title: Individual Contributions
introduction: This chapter documents each team member's independent investigation within assigned algorithm families. Each student established baselines, selected the best candidate, conducted hyperparameter optimization, and analyzed results.

sections.title: Student 1: Ensemble Methods Investigation
sections.content_html:
Student 1 investigated ensemble methods—algorithms combining multiple base learners for improved robustness (Breiman, 1996).

Baseline Comparison: Five methods were evaluated: RandomForestClassifier, BaggingClassifier, AdaBoostClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier, and ExtraTreesClassifier. BaggingClassifier achieved highest baseline balanced accuracy (90.82%).

Model Selection: BaggingClassifier was selected for its theoretical foundation (variance reduction through bootstrap aggregating), interpretable hyperparameters, and computational efficiency through parallelization.

Optimization: Grid search identified optimal configuration: n_estimators=150 (diminishing returns beyond this), max_samples=0.85 (balancing diversity and tree strength), and standard bootstrap sampling.

Results: Balanced accuracy improved from 90.82% to 91.60% (+0.78 points), MCC from 0.8076 to 0.8244. Bias-variance decomposition showed optimal balance (bias=0.0966, variance=0.0255).

Key Insight: Pure bagging outperformed boosting variants, suggesting NSL-KDD benefits more from variance reduction than sequential error correction.

sections.title: Student 2: Non-Linear Methods Investigation
sections.content_html:
Student 2 investigated non-linear methods capable of capturing complex relationships (Breiman et al., 1984; Quinlan, 1993).

Baseline Comparison: Four methods evaluated: DecisionTreeClassifier (90.50% balanced accuracy), MLPClassifier (89.12%), KNeighborsClassifier (88.41%), and GaussianNB (77.12%). GaussianNB's poor performance confirmed conditional independence assumption is violated.

Model Selection: DecisionTreeClassifier selected for highest performance, inherent interpretability (traceable decision paths), computational efficiency, and no preprocessing requirements.

Optimization: Grid search identified max_depth=20 as optimal—deep enough for nuanced patterns while preventing overfitting. Default values for min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf proved optimal.

Results: Balanced accuracy improved from 90.50% to 91.19% (+0.69 points), achieving within 0.41 points of ensemble method. Bias-variance showed lowest bias (0.0868) among all models with moderate variance (0.0331).

Key Insight: Single well-tuned decision tree achieves near-ensemble performance while offering interpretability and 90x faster training (0.87s vs 79s).

sections.title: Student 3: Support Vector Methods Investigation
sections.content_html:
Student 3 investigated linear support vector methods seeking optimal separating hyperplanes (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995; Hoerl & Kennard, 1970).

Baseline Comparison: Four linear methods evaluated: RidgeClassifier (78.76%), LinearSVC (78.90%), SGDClassifier (78.12%), and PassiveAggressiveClassifier (77.21%). Consistent performance across methods indicated fundamental linear separability limitations.

Model Selection: RidgeClassifier selected for training efficiency (closed-form solution), stable convergence, and simple regularization (single alpha parameter).

Optimization: Grid search found default alpha=1.0 optimal—model is underfitting, not overfitting. class_weight='balanced' provided most impactful improvement by addressing class imbalance.

Results: Balanced accuracy improved marginally from 78.76% to 79.18% (+0.42 points). Bias-variance decomposition confirmed severe underfitting: bias=0.2276 (more than double other models), variance=0.0045. The 12+ point gap from non-linear methods represents fundamental capacity limitations.

Key Insight: Consistent underperformance across all linear methods definitively establishes that NSL-KDD attack patterns are not linearly separable. This negative result provides clear guidance against linear methods for this problem.

sections.title: Cross-Student Synthesis
sections.content_html:
Key Findings Across Investigations:

  • Non-Linear Methods Essential: Both ensemble (91.60%) and decision tree (91.19%) achieved 91%+ accuracy, while linear methods plateaued at 79%—a consistent 12+ point gap confirming non-linear boundaries are essential.
  • Optimization Provides Modest Gains: All three investigations achieved 0.4-0.8 point improvements, suggesting algorithm selection matters more than parameter fine-tuning.
  • Distinct Bias-Variance Profiles: Ensemble achieves lowest variance through averaging; decision trees achieve lowest bias through flexible partitioning; linear methods suffer from high bias.
